GoodTrust vs Everplans (2026)

By the Afterkeep research team · Reviewed on 15 Oct 2026

Short answer: GoodTrust is the better pick if you need US legal documents: its US$149 Estate+ plan includes a will, trust and directives valid in all 50 US states, plus a Digital Vault. Everplans is a better organiser and sharing vault, free for up to 3 items or US$99.99 a year for Premium, but it doesn't create legal documents.

Key facts

  • Verdict: Pick GoodTrust to make a US will or trust and record digital assets in one place.
  • GoodTrust: Estate+ plan advertised at $149 (US). Check current pricing.
  • Everplans: Free base app; Everplans Premium is paid. Check current pricing.

Which should you choose?

Verdict: Pick GoodTrust to make a US will or trust and record digital assets in one place. Pick Everplans to organise documents, accounts and wishes and share them with family. Australians should get legal documents locally either way.

GoodTrust

An all-in-one US estate planning platform: will, trust and directives (valid in all 50 states) plus a Digital Vault for your digital life.

Everplans

A well-structured digital vault for life admin and end-of-life plans that you can securely share with people you trust.

Frequently asked questions

GoodTrust vs Everplans: which is better?

GoodTrust is the better pick if you need US legal documents: its US$149 Estate+ plan includes a will, trust and directives valid in all 50 US states, plus a Digital Vault. Everplans is a better organiser and sharing vault, free for up to 3 items or US$99.99 a year for Premium, but it doesn't create legal documents.

Is GoodTrust or Everplans better for wills?

GoodTrust. It creates US wills and trusts; Everplans doesn't create legal documents.

How much do GoodTrust and Everplans cost?

GoodTrust's Estate+ plan is listed at US$149. Everplans is free for up to 3 items, and Premium is US$99.99 a year. Prices are from each company's pricing page and may change.

Do they work in Australia?

GoodTrust's documents are for the 50 US states. Everplans can organise information anywhere, but its guidance is US-oriented. Australians should make their will under local law.

Do I still need a password manager?

Yes. Neither replaces a password manager with emergency access for day-to-day logins.
